chapters.title: Chapter 4: Adding a Risk-Free Asset: The Capital Market Line

lessons.title: The Capital Market Line and the Case for One Optimal Risky Portfolio

children.text: Lesson 2 ended on a striking claim: every investor sharing the same expectations should hold the exact same risky portfolio, the tangency portfolio, differing only in how much of their capital sits in it. This lesson pushes that claim one step further and asks what that shared portfolio has to actually be.

body.text: If every investor holds the same risky portfolio in the same relative proportions, then added together, their combined holdings must equal every risky asset that exists, each held in proportion to its market value. The tangency portfolio, under this logic, has to be the entire market.

children.text: Follow the logic through. Every investor puts some fraction of their money in the tangency portfolio, and the rest in the risk-free asset. Nobody holds any OTHER combination of risky assets, since Lesson 2 showed that would mean a flatter, worse CAL. Add up every investor's risky holdings across the entire market. Since they are all just different-sized copies of the same underlying mix, the total has to be that same mix too, scaled up to the size of the whole market. But the total of everyone's holdings, by definition, is every share of every company that exists, each one held by somebody. The only way both statements can be true at once is if the tangency portfolio IS the market: every risky asset, in exactly the proportion its total market value represents.

markDefs.definition: The specific Capital Allocation Line built using the market portfolio, every risky asset held in proportion to its market value, as the risky asset combined with the risk-free rate.

children.text: Approximating the Market Portfolio in India

The true market portfolio, every risky asset that exists, listed equity, unlisted equity, real estate, gold, even human capital, is not something anyone can actually observe or buy. This gap between theory and reality is well known enough to have a name, Roll's critique, after economist Richard Roll, who pointed out that CAPM can never be properly tested since the true market portfolio is unobservable. In practice, broad equity indices stand in as the closest available proxy: Nifty 50 for large-cap Indian equity, Nifty 500 for a wider slice of the listed market, each available as a low-cost index fund or ETF on NSE.
Worked Example: an Illustrative Nifty 50 CML

Using an illustrative long-run Nifty 50 return of 13% and risk of 16%, with Rf = 6.5% as in earlier lessons of this chapter, the market Sharpe ratio, and CML slope, works out to (13 - 6.5) / 16 = 0.406.

children.text: Follow this chapter's logic all the way through, and it delivers one of the most consequential conclusions in all of finance. If every investor shares the same beliefs about returns, risk, and correlations, then the theoretically optimal strategy for every single one of them is identical: hold a broad market index fund, and choose only how much to allocate between it and the risk-free asset. Under these assumptions, Chapter 3's entire exercise, building a custom five-stock efficient frontier, adds no value at all over simply buying a Nifty 50 index fund and a T-Bill in the right proportion. This is the theoretical backbone of the case for passive, index-fund investing.

body.text: That conclusion rests entirely on assumptions this chapter has already flagged as unrealistic: every investor sharing identical expected returns, variances, and covariances, with no transaction costs, taxes, or borrowing frictions. Real investors disagree, sometimes because they have genuinely better information or analysis, sometimes because they simply hold different, equally reasonable views. Chapter 3's custom frontier-building is not rendered pointless by this lesson. It is exactly what an investor who believes their own estimates of return and risk differ from the market's consensus should be doing instead of defaulting to the index. Chapter 5 covers where those custom estimates themselves tend to go wrong.

body.title: CAL versus CML
body.question: What is the actual difference between a general Capital Allocation Line (Lesson 1) and the Capital Market Line (this lesson)?
options: There is no real difference, the two terms are interchangeable
A CAL always has a steeper slope than the CML
The CML is the one specific CAL that uses the market portfolio (the tangency/equilibrium portfolio) as its risky asset; a general CAL can be built from ANY risky portfolio, efficient or not
The CML only applies to bonds, while the CAL only applies to equities
body.explanation: A CAL is a general concept: risk-free asset plus any risky portfolio, even a poorly chosen one. The CML is the specific, special case where that risky portfolio is the market portfolio, which under this chapter's equilibrium argument is also the tangency portfolio, making the CML the single steepest CAL there is.

cards.definition: Every risky asset that exists, held in proportion to its total market value. The tangency portfolio, under the assumption that all investors share the same beliefs.
The specific Capital Allocation Line built using the market portfolio as its risky asset.
The observation, from economist Richard Roll, that the true market portfolio cannot be observed or fully constructed in practice, making the CML and CAPM difficult to test directly.

points: If every investor holds the same tangency portfolio in the same relative proportions, their combined holdings must equal the entire market, which means the tangency portfolio IS the market portfolio under this chapter's assumptions.
The Capital Market Line is the specific CAL built from the market portfolio, distinct from a general CAL, which can be built from any risky portfolio.
The true market portfolio cannot be fully observed or constructed, a limitation known as Roll's critique. Broad equity indices like Nifty 50 or Nifty 500 serve as the standard practical proxy.
Under strict CAPM assumptions, the theoretically optimal strategy for every investor is identical: hold a market index fund, and adjust only the split between it and the risk-free asset.
This is the formal theoretical case for passive, index-fund investing, and it depends entirely on every investor sharing the same beliefs, an assumption real markets routinely violate.

Custom portfolio construction, like Chapter 3's five-stock frontier, remains justified for investors who genuinely believe their own estimates differ from the market consensus, not rendered pointless by this lesson's result.
